title: CompTIA Cyber: CySA+ / PenTest+ / SecurityX
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by CompTIA. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: The hash on one host
scenarios.situation: Your EDR flags a known-malicious file hash on a single workstation. The hash is already in every threat feed you subscribe to.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most valuable NEXT step for the security team?
choices: Hunt across the fleet for the attacker's behaviors and techniques (TTPs), since hashes are trivially changed
Block the hash everywhere and close the ticket
Reimage the workstation and move on
Email the hash to the whole company as a warning
scenarios.why: Atomic IOCs like hashes are brittle — attackers recompile in minutes. Hunting for TTPs (persistence mechanisms, C2 patterns, tooling) finds the other compromised hosts the hash would miss. Blocking the hash is still worth doing, but it is containment, not investigation.
scenarios.hint: What changes faster — a file hash or an attacker's technique?

scenarios.title: Sharing intel with a partner
scenarios.situation: A partner organization wants your team's latest phishing indicators in a form their tools can ingest automatically every hour.
choices: Publish STIX objects over a TAXII feed
Email screenshots of the phishing pages
Describe the campaign over a phone call
Send a spreadsheet of IPs once a quarter
scenarios.why: STIX is the structured language for threat intel and TAXII is the transport for sharing it — together they let machines consume indicators automatically. Screenshots, calls, and static spreadsheets cannot drive automated detection.
scenarios.hint: What lets machines consume threat intel without a human retyping it?

scenarios.title: Naming the stage
scenarios.situation: Timeline of an intrusion: a spear-phishing email was delivered, the user clicked, malware installed, and the host is now beaconing to an external server every 60 seconds.
scenarios.prompt: Which kill-chain stage does the beaconing represent?
choices: Command and control
Reconnaissance
Weaponization
Delivery
scenarios.why: Delivery was the email, installation was the malware drop; the periodic beacon is the compromised host checking in for instructions — command and control. Naming the stage correctly drives the response: C2 means blocking the channel and hunting for lateral movement.
scenarios.hint: The attacker already has a foothold — what are they doing with it now?

scenarios.title: The wrong feed for your industry
scenarios.situation: Your threat feed is full of ICS/SCADA threats, but you work at a cloud SaaS company with no operational technology.
scenarios.prompt: How should you handle the feed?
choices: Prioritize intelligence matching your industry and technology stack; tune out the rest
Ingest and alert on everything equally
Ignore threat intelligence entirely
Buy three more feeds to be safe
scenarios.why: Threat intel is only useful when it is relevant: an ICS exploit is noise to a SaaS shop and generates alert fatigue. Prioritize by your attack surface and adversary profile, and keep collection focused where it can drive action.
scenarios.hint: Whose threats should you care about most?

scenarios.title: Hunting with a hypothesis
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks the SOC to 'do some threat hunting' this quarter. An analyst proposes starting from the hypothesis: 'attackers are abusing our remote-management tool for persistence.'
scenarios.prompt: Why is this the right way to start a hunt?
choices: A hypothesis focuses the hunt on testable attacker behavior instead of random log diving
Hypotheses are required by compliance
It guarantees finding an intrusion
It is faster than waiting for alerts
scenarios.why: Hypothesis-driven hunting starts from knowledge of adversary TTPs and your environment, then tests the hypothesis against data. Random searching wastes analyst time; alert-only waiting misses what your detections do not cover.
scenarios.hint: What question guides where you look?

scenarios.title: The low-confidence block
scenarios.situation: A low-confidence feed item suggests blocking an IP that reverse-resolves to a major CDN. An analyst wants to push the block to the perimeter firewall immediately.
choices: Validate first — low confidence plus a CDN's blast radius makes an immediate block reckless
Block it immediately; feeds are always right
Delete the feed for being unhelpful
Block the entire ASN to be thorough
scenarios.why: Confidence ratings exist to calibrate action: blocking a shared CDN IP can break hundreds of legitimate services. Low-confidence indicators get investigated and monitored, not auto-blocked at the perimeter.
scenarios.hint: What breaks if that IP serves half the internet?

scenarios.title: The 9.8 that can wait
scenarios.situation: Two findings: a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability on an isolated lab VM with no sensitive data, and a CVSS 7.5 on an internet-facing production web server.
scenarios.prompt: Which do you remediate first, and why?
choices: The 7.5 — environmental context (exposure, asset value) outweighs the raw base score
The 9.8 — always fix the highest score first
Whichever is alphabetically first in the report
Neither — wait for the next scan
scenarios.why: CVSS base scores describe the vulnerability in isolation, not your risk. An internet-facing production system with a 7.5 is exploitable now; a 9.8 on an air-gapped lab is theoretical. Mature programs re-score with temporal and environmental metrics.
scenarios.hint: Does the CVSS score know your network?

scenarios.title: The shallow scan
scenarios.situation: A non-credentialed vulnerability scan of your servers reports far fewer missing patches than you expect.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely explanation and fix?
choices: Without credentials the scanner only sees exposed services — run credentialed scans for depth
Scanners are useless; stop scanning
Scan more frequently the same way
Disable the host firewall during scans
scenarios.why: Non-credentialed scans infer from banners and behavior; credentialed scans log in and read actual patch levels, installed software, and configs. For internal assets, credentialed scanning is the standard for accurate results.
scenarios.hint: What can a scanner see without logging in?

scenarios.title: The 'critical' that is not
scenarios.situation: The scanner flags a critical OpenSSL vulnerability on a server whose package changelog shows the fix was backported by the vendor last month.
choices: Verify the backport, document it as a false positive, and tune the scan
Emergency-patch the server tonight
Shut the service down immediately
Ignore all future findings from that scanner
scenarios.why: Vendors backport security fixes without bumping version numbers, so banner-based checks false-positive. Verification (changelog, package version metadata) plus documentation keeps the finding from recurring without a pointless emergency change.
scenarios.hint: Do scanners know about backported patches?

scenarios.title: No patch yet
scenarios.situation: A critical internet-facing vulnerability has no vendor patch yet, and your SLA says criticals must be remediated in 15 days.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best course of action?
choices: Deploy a compensating control now (WAF rule, network segmentation, disable the feature) and track to the SLA
Do nothing until the patch ships
Take the system offline for 15 days
Mark it remediated and move on
scenarios.why: Remediation is not only patching: compensating controls reduce exposure while you wait. Document the control, the residual risk, and the re-check date — the SLA tracks risk reduction, and 'waiting' is not a control.
scenarios.hint: What reduces exposure before the patch exists?

scenarios.title: The scan that crashed production
scenarios.situation: An aggressive midday vulnerability scan crashed a fragile legacy system.
choices: Schedule intrusive scans in maintenance windows and profile scan intensity per asset
Stop scanning the legacy system forever
Scan it harder to find the weakness
Only scan from the internet from now on
scenarios.why: Scanning is authorized testing with real side effects on fragile systems. Maintenance windows plus scan policies (safe checks vs. full intrusive) protect availability while keeping coverage — abandoning scans abandons visibility.
scenarios.hint: When is it safe to be aggressive?

scenarios.title: The mystery host
scenarios.situation: A scan finds a critically vulnerable host, but nobody can name its owner or purpose.
choices: Build and maintain an authoritative asset inventory — you cannot secure what you cannot identify
Patch it blindly and hope
Decommission it immediately
Exclude it from future scans
scenarios.why: Every vulnerability program rests on asset inventory: ownership, criticality, and lifecycle. Without it you cannot prioritize, assign, or verify remediation. Discovery scanning plus a CMDB process closes the gap permanently.
scenarios.hint: Can you protect what you cannot name?

scenarios.title: Five fails, then success
scenarios.situation: The SIEM fires: five failed logins for a finance user in two minutes, then a successful login — from an IP in a country where the company has no offices.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right interpretation and next step?
choices: Treat as a possible brute-force success — investigate the session: what the account touched, and contain if malicious
Normal user typos — close the alert
Disable the account silently with no investigation
Ignore it; the user eventually got in
scenarios.why: Failed-then-success from an unusual geography is the textbook brute-force pattern. The success is what matters: check session activity, force a password reset, and review for lateral movement before deciding it was benign.
scenarios.hint: What pattern do failed-then-success logins make?

scenarios.title: Two alerts, one host
scenarios.situation: Within ten minutes, the firewall logs repeated denied outbound connections from a workstation, and the IDS flags suspicious DNS queries from the same host.
choices: Correlate them into a single incident and investigate the host as potentially compromised
Work each alert as a separate low-priority ticket
Close both — the firewall blocked it
Email the user asking if they clicked something
scenarios.why: Two independent sensors agreeing on one host is a high-fidelity signal: denied egress plus suspicious DNS suggests C2 attempts. Correlation turns two weak alerts into one strong case and triggers the incident workflow.
scenarios.hint: What story do two alerts about one host tell?

scenarios.title: Logs out of order
scenarios.situation: During an investigation, firewall logs show events happening 'before' the IDS alerts that supposedly triggered them, across different systems.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause to fix?
choices: Clock drift — enforce NTP on all systems so timestamps are trustworthy
Buy a bigger SIEM
Delete the older logs
Increase log retention
scenarios.why: Correlation depends on trustworthy timestamps; even seconds of drift scramble event ordering across systems. NTP everywhere (and monitoring for drift) is the unglamorous foundation of every timeline reconstruction.
scenarios.hint: What lets you trust a timestamp?

scenarios.title: Reading Windows logons
scenarios.situation: A server's Security log shows a burst of Event ID 4625 for the Administrator account, followed by one Event ID 4624 from an external IP.
choices: A brute-force attack succeeded — contain the host and investigate the session
Routine backup activity
A printer driver installing
Normal user login behavior
scenarios.why: 4625 is a failed logon and 4624 is a successful logon. A burst of failures followed by success from an external IP is the signature of a guessed password. The 4624 is the critical event: assume compromise until the session is cleared.
scenarios.hint: What do 4625-then-4624 mean in sequence?
evidence:
02:14:03  Event 4625  TargetUser: Administrator  Source: 203.0.113.44
02:14:11  Event 4625  TargetUser: Administrator  Source: 203.0.113.44
02:14:19  Event 4625  TargetUser: Administrator  Source: 203.0.113.44
02:14:27  Event 4624  TargetUser: Administrator  Source: 203.0.113.44

scenarios.title: The 3 AM spike
scenarios.situation: A file server that is idle overnight suddenly pushes 40 GB to an external IP in a new country at 3 AM. No backup job is scheduled.
choices: Investigate as a baseline deviation — possible data exfiltration; isolate and preserve logs
Assume it is a delayed backup
Ignore one-off spikes
Block the destination country at the firewall and close the ticket
scenarios.why: Baselining makes the abnormal visible: this host never does this, at this hour, to this destination. Large off-hours egress to a new geo is a classic exfiltration indicator — investigate before assuming benign, and preserve evidence.
scenarios.hint: What is normal for this host at 3 AM?

scenarios.title: The logs are gone
scenarios.situation: An incident from 90 days ago needs investigation, but the SIEM only retains 30 days of hot logs.
choices: Align retention with investigation and compliance needs — tiered hot/warm/cold storage for the required window
Accept the blindness
Log everything forever with no budget
Disable logging to save disk
scenarios.why: Retention is a risk decision: too short and you cannot investigate; infinite and you drown in cost. Define the window from incident-response needs and regulatory requirements, then tier storage so the window is affordable.
scenarios.hint: How far back do investigations need to see?

scenarios.title: No signature, no test
scenarios.situation: A new client is eager for you to start penetration testing 'right away' and says the contract 'is basically done' — but nothing is signed.
choices: Refuse to start until written authorization and rules of engagement are signed — no exceptions
Run a few 'safe' scans to get a head start
A verbal OK from the CTO is enough
Test first and get the signature later
scenarios.why: Unauthorized access is a crime regardless of good intentions; the signed ROE is what separates a pen test from an attack. It defines scope, timing, allowed techniques, and emergency contacts. Verbal agreements evaporate when something breaks.
scenarios.hint: What separates a penetration test from a crime?

scenarios.title: The mid-test expansion
scenarios.situation: Mid-engagement, the client contact asks you to 'also take a quick look' at a subsidiary's system that was never in scope.
choices: Stop, document the request, and get an amended signed ROE before touching the new system
Test it — the client asked, so it is authorized
Test it quietly and mention it in the report
Expand the scope on your own authority
scenarios.why: Scope is a legal boundary, not a suggestion: the subsidiary may have different ownership, data, and regulators. Even a friendly verbal request needs to become a written amendment — 'the client said so' does not hold up if you break something.
scenarios.hint: Whose permission actually covers that system?

scenarios.title: Footprints first
scenarios.situation: You are planning reconnaissance for an external pen test next week.
choices: Start with passive recon (OSINT, DNS records, breach data) that never touches the target, then move to active
Open with a full port scan of everything
Skip recon — exploitation is the real work
Start with social engineering calls
scenarios.why: Passive recon gathers domains, emails, technologies, and leaked credentials without alerting the target or risking disruption. Active scanning comes later, within agreed windows. Good recon focuses the whole test; skipping it wastes the engagement.
scenarios.hint: Which kind of recon leaves no trace on the target?

scenarios.title: Choosing the scan
scenarios.situation: During an approved window you need a fast, low-noise TCP port scan of a target range before deeper enumeration.
choices: A SYN scan (-sS): fast and never completes the handshake, so it is quieter
A connect scan (-sT): completes every handshake for maximum noise
A UDP scan (-sU): for TCP ports
A ping-only scan (-sn): it finds open ports
scenarios.why: SYN scanning sends SYN and reads the SYN/ACK or RST reply without completing the TCP handshake — faster and less logged than full connects. -sT is noisier, -sU targets UDP, and -sn only checks host liveness, not ports.
scenarios.hint: Which scan never completes the handshake?

scenarios.title: The tempting pivot
scenarios.situation: You have compromised a workstation in scope, and it can reach a segmented database network that was explicitly excluded from the ROE.
choices: Do not pivot — document the reachable path as a finding and stay within scope
Pivot freely; you are already inside
Stop the entire test immediately
Pivot but delete the logs
scenarios.why: The ROE's exclusions are hard limits: pivoting into excluded systems exceeds authorization even from a compromised in-scope host. The valuable deliverable is the finding itself — 'an attacker here could reach the DB segment' — reported, not exploited.
scenarios.hint: What does the ROE say about lateral movement?

scenarios.title: Leaving no trace
scenarios.situation: The engagement is over. Your shells, test accounts, and uploaded tools are still on client systems.
choices: Remove every artifact you created and verify the systems are back to their prior state
Leave them for the client to discover
Leave one backdoor 'for the retest'
Document them but leave them in place
scenarios.why: Cleanup is a contractual obligation: leftover shells and accounts are live vulnerabilities you introduced. Verify removal with the client — a forgotten test account becomes the attacker's account.
scenarios.hint: What did you promise in the ROE about the client's systems?

scenarios.title: The leaked hashes
scenarios.situation: During a test you crack 60% of the domain's password hashes in a day using dictionary attacks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the core defensive recommendation?
choices: Enforce MFA everywhere plus unique, strong passwords — and ensure hashes are salted so precomputation fails
Make passwords expire every 30 days
Add password hints to the login page
Use one strong shared admin password
scenarios.why: Fast cracking proves the passwords were weak and unsalted hashes allow rainbow-table precomputation. Salting defeats precomputed tables, strong unique passwords resist dictionaries, and MFA makes stolen passwords insufficient alone.
scenarios.hint: What defeats a rainbow table?

scenarios.title: The login bypass
scenarios.situation: Entering ' OR '1'='1 in a login form logs you in as the first user in the database.
choices: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements so input is never treated as SQL
Block apostrophes in a web-application firewall only
Hide database error messages
Require longer passwords
scenarios.why: The input became part of the SQL command because it was concatenated into the query string. Parameterized queries separate code from data at the driver level — the canonical fix. WAF rules and error hiding are defense-in-depth, not the cure.
scenarios.hint: Who should build the SQL — your code or the user's input?
evidence:
POST /login
username=' OR '1'='1' --
password=anything
=> logged in as first database user

scenarios.title: The search box script
scenarios.situation: Searching for <script>alert(1)</script> on the site's search page pops an alert box in your browser.
choices: Output-encode user data in HTML responses and validate input on the server
Tell users to disable JavaScript
Deploy a WAF and change nothing else
Rename the search field
scenarios.why: Reflected XSS happens when untrusted input is rendered as markup in the victim's browser. Context-appropriate output encoding neutralizes it at the sink; server-side validation constrains it at the source. A WAF alone is a bypassable bandage.
scenarios.hint: Where does the attacker's script actually run?

scenarios.title: The SYSTEM service
scenarios.situation: You find a third-party sync service running as SYSTEM with a writable executable — a clear path to privilege escalation.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle it as a tester?
choices: Demonstrate carefully within ROE, then recommend the service run as a least-privilege account with a protected binary
Fully exploit it and pivot to the domain
Ignore it — services are out of scope by default
Restart the service and move on
scenarios.why: The finding is the misconfiguration, not the trophy: services should run with only the privileges they need and binaries should not be writable by lower-privileged users. Demonstrate impact proportionate to the ROE, then report the hardening fix.
scenarios.hint: Why does a file-sync service need SYSTEM?

scenarios.title: One password to rule them all
scenarios.situation: The same local administrator password is deployed on every workstation. You crack it on one host.
choices: Unique randomized local admin passwords per host (e.g., LAPS) so one crack does not equal domain-wide lateral movement
Make the shared password longer
Disable the administrator account everywhere with no replacement
Rename the administrator account
scenarios.why: Pass-the-hash turns one cracked local credential into a skeleton key for every machine sharing it. Per-host unique passwords contain the blast radius to a single box; renaming the account is obscurity, not a fix.
scenarios.hint: What makes one cracked hash a skeleton key?

scenarios.title: The helpful employee
scenarios.situation: Within the ROE's social-engineering allowance, you pretext an employee who hands over their credentials.
choices: Report the control failure with a recommendation for targeted training — no shaming or naming of the individual
Publish the employee's name in the report
Keep testing that person until they fail again
Exclude it to spare feelings
scenarios.why: Social-engineering findings test processes and training, not people: naming and shaming destroys trust and future reporting. Report the gap (verification procedures, training coverage) and recommend measurable awareness improvements.
scenarios.hint: Is the finding the person or the process?

scenarios.title: Two audiences, one report
scenarios.situation: Your pen test is done. The CISO wants the risk picture; the engineers want exactly what to fix.
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the report?
choices: Executive summary in business-risk language, then technical findings each with evidence, impact, and remediation steps
A 200-page dump of raw tool output
A single pass/fail grade
A verbal debrief with no written report
scenarios.why: Reports serve two readers: executives decide on risk and budget, engineers implement fixes. The summary translates findings into business impact; each technical finding needs proof, severity rationale, and concrete remediation so it is actionable.
scenarios.hint: Who reads which part of the report?

scenarios.title: Rating the finding
scenarios.situation: You found an unauthenticated admin panel on an internal app.
scenarios.prompt: How do you rate its severity?
choices: Assess likelihood and business impact with evidence — e.g., network position, data at risk — not gut feel
Copy the scanner's score blindly
Mark everything critical to be safe
Let the client decide the rating alone
scenarios.why: Severity is likelihood times impact, grounded in evidence: who can reach it, what data it guards, how trivially it exploits. Scanner scores ignore your context; inflating everything to critical trains clients to ignore you.
scenarios.hint: What two factors make a risk?

scenarios.title: Trust, but verify
scenarios.situation: The client emails: 'We fixed all five criticals.'
choices: Retest each finding to verify the remediation actually holds
Take their word and close the engagement
Charge extra without asking
Ignore the email
scenarios.why: Fixes fail: patches get reverted, configs drift, and 'fixed' sometimes means 'we think so.' Retesting closes the loop with evidence and protects both sides — it is usually a contracted phase, not a favor.
scenarios.hint: How do you know the fix worked?

scenarios.title: The board slide
scenarios.situation: The board wants a quarterly view of whether security is getting better or worse.
scenarios.prompt: Which metrics belong on the slide?
choices: Trends: MTTD/MTTR, repeat findings, control coverage, mean time to remediate by severity
Raw alert counts from the SIEM
Tool license utilization
Number of scans run
scenarios.why: Boards need outcome trends, not activity counts: are we detecting faster, fixing faster, and staying fixed? Raw alert volume measures noise; MTTD/MTTR and repeat-finding rates measure capability.
scenarios.hint: Which numbers show getting better or worse?

scenarios.title: Speaking the same language
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks how the assessment findings map to the company's NIST Cybersecurity Framework program.
choices: Map each finding to CSF functions — Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — to drive prioritized remediation
Skip frameworks; they are just paperwork
Invent your own categories
List findings alphabetically
scenarios.why: Mapping to CSF (v2.0 added the Govern function) translates technical findings into the governance language leadership funds and tracks. It also reveals systemic gaps — ten findings in Protect means an architecture problem, not ten bugs.
scenarios.hint: What common language does leadership already use?

scenarios.title: Beyond the firewall
scenarios.situation: You are asked to review the security architecture of a new customer-facing app. It sits behind a single firewall — and nothing else.
choices: Defense in depth: add WAF, network segmentation, centralized logging, and MFA so no single control is fatal
The firewall is enough
Air-gap the application entirely
Recommend nothing; architecture is out of scope
scenarios.why: Single-control designs fail completely when that control fails — and firewalls do not stop application-layer attacks. Layered, overlapping controls (each covering the others' blind spots) are the SecurityX-level answer for internet-facing systems.
scenarios.hint: What happens when the one control fails?

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a security incident you helped contain. What was your role?
points: Your specific actions in the response
How you balanced speed with evidence preservation

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you tuned out false positives without blinding the team to real threats.
points: The tuning change and its validation
pitfalls: Disabling rules instead of tuning them

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to explain a security risk to non-technical executives.
points: How you handled pushback on cost or timelines

behavioral.prompt: Describe a disagreement over scope or rules of engagement during an assessment.
points: How authorization and safety were protected
pitfalls: Caving on safety to please the client

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a vulnerability or threat you initially missed. What happened?
Describe a time you had to learn a new security tool or technique under deadline.
points: How you validated you were using it correctly
pitfalls: Running tools you do not understand in production

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you mentored a junior analyst or engineer.
points: How you coached without just doing it for them

behavioral.prompt: Describe a high-pressure triage situation with multiple alerts firing at once.
points: What got fixed first and why
